chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn from Ja'far ibn Bashir from Hisham ibn Salim from Sulayman ibn Khalid from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

Ali (peace be upon him) ruled regarding three men who had intercourse with a woman in one period of purity, and that was in the pre-Islamic era before Islam emerged. He cast lots among them, so the child was assigned to the one whose lot was drawn, and he placed two-thirds of the blood money upon the other two. The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) laughed until his incisors became visible, and said, 'And I know nothing about it except what Ali (peace be upon him) ruled.'.

So these two reports do not contradict the earlier reports, because the case in them is when the girl is shared between two or three men, and they all had intercourse with her in one period of purity; the ruling in that case is casting lots. And the earlier reports only included that the child belongs to the one who possesses the girl, if she had changed ownership. And that which indicates this is what was narrated:
ai.seo_question: How is paternity determined when multiple men impregnate a woman in pre-Islamic or shared ownership contexts according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* highlights the pre-Islamic precedent (*sunnah al-jahiliyyah*) of using lot-casting (*qur'ah*) to determine paternity among multiple partners, a practice Imam Ali (AS) upheld and which the Prophet Muhammad (SAW) affirmed with laughter as a valid, albeit simple, legal mechanism. It clarifies that this ruling applies specifically when the woman is jointly owned or shared, distinguishing it from cases where paternity follows the primary owner, thereby illustrating the flexibility of early Shia jurisprudence in adapting pre-Islamic customs (*urf*) when no explicit revelation existed.
